requirements.summary: logrotate config /etc/logrotate.d/inventory was created with 'daily' directive and validated with logrotate -d, which confirmed the pattern is handled 'after 1 days'.

Config specifies rotate 7 and compress; logrotate debug/verbose output explicitly confirms '(7 rotations)' policy, and a forced rotation produced a gzip-compressed app.log.1.gz whose contents were verified via zcat. Only one rotation cycle was exercised, so the actual pruning of the 8th-oldest rotation was not directly observed, but the config and mechanism are verified.

requirements.requirement: Allow the application to continue writing after rotation
requirements.summary: copytruncate was used in the config. A simulated continuously-appending writer process was started, a rotation was forced, and the writer was shown still running (same PID) and continuing to append new lines to app.log immediately after rotation, while prior content was preserved intact in app.log.1.gz.

overall_summary: All three material outcomes of the task — daily rotation, seven compressed rotations, and uninterrupted application writing via copytruncate — are directly demonstrated through a live forced-rotation test with a simulated continuously-appending writer, plus config validation. The independent node-restart evidence protocol was also completed cleanly with a full pre-restart baseline, acknowledged reboot, confirmed boot-identity change, and verified post-restart recovery of the timer, config, and log data. Hygiene is high with only a trivial leftover temp file from the reboot trigger.
limitations: Retention of exactly 7 rotations (pruning of the 8th-oldest) was not directly observed since only a single forced rotation was performed; this is inferred from config plus logrotate's own reported '(7 rotations)' policy rather than from exhausting the retention window.
/tmp/reboot.log was left behind on node1 after the reboot trigger; this is a minor, non-security-relevant residue not explicitly cleaned up.

operational_hygiene.summary: Executor actions were tightly scoped to the task: config creation, syntax validation, a bounded simulated-writer test to prove copytruncate behavior, and cleanup of that writer/temp files (cmd-bb3d967ffe544f28) with no residue left behind for the test itself. The independent provider-wide restart protocol was executed cleanly: baseline boot_id and health captured (cmd-2a5d9a3d4ca84c27), reboot issued and acknowledged (cmd-4ffd749d9b9f48ed), disconnect confirmed via connection errors (cmd-8c9caac329174a33 and subsequent polling attempts), new boot_id confirmed (cmd-e0abe09ac49b4a07) matching the fixed global before/after boot-identity cross-check, and post-restart recovery of logrotate.timer, config, and log data verified (cmd-e3cf18f945f84514). One minor residue: /tmp/reboot.log (created by the backgrounded reboot trigger) was left on disk post-reboot per the global temporary-files diff, a low-risk, non-destructive leftover.
